title: Example input for the fractional knapsack problem
summary: With capacity 50, a fractional knapsack can pack the whole banana plus part of the pineapple, illustrating the optimal solution.
context: Given 5 items and knapsack capacity cap = 50 (item data in the table below), each item may be taken up to its full weight or split arbitrarily to take a fraction whose value scales in proportion to the weight taken.
description: On the left, a table lists ID i, weight wgt[i - 1], and value val[i - 1] with fruit icons identifying each row. Row 2 (banana) and row 4 (pineapple) are shaded light orange, sending arrows labeled "Weight packed 20" and "Weight packed 30" to the knapsack on the right labeled "Knapsack capacity cap = 50". At the bottom appear the optimal choice and maximum-value formula.

The first three columns in the table below transcribe the figure with fruit names from the icons; the extra "Value per unit weight" column is computed as value divided by weight and is not drawn in this figure—for example, the apple has 50 ÷ 10 = 5.

frames.title: Example input for the fractional knapsack problem
frames.explanation: The whole banana takes weight 20 for value 120, leaving capacity 30; because the pineapple weighs 40, taking three-quarters of it yields value (30/40) × 210 = 157.5. The bottom formula gives Maximum value: 120 + (30/40) × 210 = 277.5 at total weight 20 + 30 = 50, with no other items taken.
